messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos was seventy, a welder who had spent forty years in the United States after fleeing torture in El Salvador. In his early twenties he had been a union organizer; paramilitaries abducted him from his home, blindfolded him, and held him for three days in a windowless cell. They beat him with rifle butts, put a pistol to his head and pulled the trigger on an empty chamber, and fired live rounds into the wall beside him. He could do nothing—his hands were bound, his mouth taped, and every noise told him he was utterly without options. The worst part, he later told himself, was that he had not fought back; he had gone limp, nodded when they demanded information he did not have. He was released, eventually, but the shame and the fury stayed.

In the decades that followed, Carlos built a quiet life—raised a daughter, worked long shifts in fabrication shops. But the triggers were everywhere. A car backfiring outside the shop would send the gunshot noise crashing through him, and the memory would arrive not as a recollection but as a present-tense assault: he could taste the grime of the blindfold, feel the cold concrete against his back, and the rage would surge so hot that his hands shook. When he tried to explain what had happened to a coworker, he would lose the thread mid-sentence and stop, the words dissolving into a jumble of images he could not sequence. That inability to describe it cleanly only deepened another conviction: the event had happened because of the way he had acted—because he had been passive, compliant—and he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop it.

His work routine became a minefield. Narrow welding booths, with their enclosed sides and limited exits, triggered the sensation of entrapment: having no options, just like in that cell. The feeling of being cornered would instantly revive the memory’s presence, and with it the gnawing fear that he could never know who would harm him next—any stranger, any coworker, any sudden noise could be a threat. To cope, Carlos developed habits that were barely conscious. When a trigger struck, he would force himself to suppress the thoughts, trying to push the images away. At the same time, he would detach from the memory, watching himself as if from a distance, numb. And when he felt threatened—say, a foreman raised his voice—Carlos would become overly compliant, nodding, agreeing, offering no resistance, the same posture he had taken in the torture chamber. The guilt he carried made this fawn response automatic: he believed that if he had acted differently then, he would not have suffered, so now he tried to preempt any danger by placating.

The hypervigilance that grew from his fear of harm turned every unexpected noise into a potential trigger, and the memory itself—so raw, so present—functioned as its own trigger, sending him into a spiral of scanning and vigilance. Over the months he began avoiding any situation that felt enclosed or unpredictable. He turned down welding jobs in tight crawl spaces. He left a grocery store once because a child’s balloon popped. At home he would sit in his armchair with the television off, trying to stay inside a bare, quiet room where no surprises could reach him.

His daughter finally insisted he see someone after he froze for ten minutes at the sound of a dropped steel beam, unable to speak or move, the memory so vivid he had not known where he was. Carlos came to the clinic afraid that his mind was broken, but also hoping—desperately, silently—that there might be a way to stop the cycle without having to stay numb forever.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not show that triggers (e.g., backfiring cars, narrow booths) directly cause negative appraisals (self-blame, guilt). The negative appraisals are presented as stable beliefs, not activated by triggers.
The vignette does not show that negative appraisals lead to triggers. Instead, hypervigilance (stemming from fear of harm) turns noises into triggers, not the self-blame itself.
